analysis.one_liner: Makes police departments pay damages when their officers violate someone's constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote, drew zero cosponsors, and died in subcommittee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change a federal civil rights law so that when a police officer violates someone's constitutional rights, the officer's government employer — typically a city or county police department — can be sued for damages, the same way a private company is liable for harm its employees cause on the job. It also blocks the employer from using the officer's personal legal immunity as a shield against those claims. It was introduced by one member, referred to a committee and then two subcommittees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of police misconduct. Under current law, winning a civil rights lawsuit often requires proving the officer acted unreasonably; if the bill passed, victims could instead sue the department for the officer's on-the-job violations and recover money even where the officer personally is shielded by legal immunity [S3]. The prospect of departments paying out judgments would also push them to screen, train, and discipline officers, which protects the broader public.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) so a law enforcement officer's government employer is vicariously liable, in the same way a private employer is liable for an employee's negligence, for the officer's on-the-job acts that deprive someone of constitutional rights [S3].
Deems any officer conduct under color of law to be within the scope of employment, so departments cannot escape liability by arguing the officer was off-task when the violation occurred [S3].

Prohibits the employer from raising the officer's immunity as a defense against the vicarious liability claim, meaning an officer's personal immunity could no longer block recovery from the department [S3].
Explicitly preserves other theories of liability, so the change adds a route to recovery without closing existing ones [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Local governments — cities, counties, and their police departments — would bear the cost of judgments and higher liability insurance, costs ultimately carried by local taxpayers. Police departments would also face stronger financial pressure to reform hiring, training, and discipline.

drawbacks.text: Because the employer is liable even when the act was unconstitutional, departments and their insurers would pay out more judgments, and those costs are ultimately passed to local taxpayers through budgets and insurance premiums [S3].

The bill targets only law enforcement officers, leaving the equivalent vicarious liability path unavailable for misconduct by other government actors, a scope limit an honest supporter would have to justify [S3].

Opponents of employer liability for police generally argue it can raise insurance costs for cash-strapped small jurisdictions and shift pressure away from holding individual officers personally accountable; the bill keeps individual suits intact but does not resolve that debate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: victims of constitutional violations would gain a reliable path to compensation, paid for by the government entities that employ the officers and, at one remove, by local taxpayers. Putting the cost on departments rather than victims is a defensible design choice, since departments are the actors positioned to prevent misconduct through training and discipline. The bill's narrow scope (law enforcement only) and lack of any co-sponsorship mean it was never tested or amended through the normal process, so its practical costs were never weighed in a hearing or a markup.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittees for the rest of the Congress, never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on March 2, 2021, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S5].

On May 18, 2021, it was referred to two Judiciary subcommittees — the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties and the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — which is as far as it ever went [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors [S4].
No further action was taken after the subcommittee referrals, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local governments, police departments, and their liability insurers are better off, since they were never required to take on the costs of paying judgments for officers' constitutional violations. People harmed by police misconduct gained nothing, and the existing legal barriers to recovering from a department remain in place.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never scheduled a markup or floor consideration for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: Not one member joined as a cosponsor across the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed [S4].

industries.note: The bill would make departments pay damages for officers' constitutional violations and face financial pressure to reform hiring, training, and discipline. Departments' interest in avoiding that liability ran against victims' interest in compensation.

More successful claims against departments would raise insurers' payouts, while higher premiums charged to cities would shift the cost to taxpayers. Their interest in limiting payouts ran against victims' recovery.
